title: Bread in the Desert
overview: When the freed Israelites run out of food and complain, God feeds them each day with quail and a strange bread called manna, teaching them daily trust and a weekly day of rest.

parts.label: Hunger and complaint (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: About a month after leaving Egypt, the food they brought with them has run out, and the people turn on Moses and Aaron. In their fear they remember slavery in Egypt as a time of full cooking pots, likely far rosier than it really was.

parts.label: A promise and a test (vv. 4-12)
parts.note: God promises meat in the evening and bread every morning, but only a day's supply at a time, to see whether the people will follow instructions and trust there will be more tomorrow. Moses points out that their complaint is really aimed at the LORD, and God's glory appears in the cloud that had been guiding them.

parts.label: Quail and manna arrive (vv. 13-21)
parts.note: Quail, birds that migrate through this region, cover the camp, and in the morning thin flakes lie on the ground; the people ask "What is it?", which in Hebrew sounds like the name manna. Everyone ends up with just enough, and any kept overnight rots, so hoarding does not work.

parts.label: A day of rest (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: On the sixth day they gather double, and that extra portion stays fresh, because on the seventh day none falls. This is the Bible's first command to keep a weekly sabbath, a day of rest set apart for the LORD, given here even before the laws at Mount Sinai.

parts.label: A jar kept for memory (vv. 31-36)
parts.note: A day's portion of manna is saved in a jar so later generations can see how they were fed, and placed beside the stone tablets of the law, which are only given later, so this part seems written looking back. Christians later read the manna in light of Jesus, who called himself the true bread from heaven.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the manna was a natural desert food that God supplied in unusual ways or an entirely miraculous provision with no natural explanation.
think: Have you ever remembered a hard past as better than it was because the present felt uncertain, and what do you think drives that?
